newsitem.title: ITALY: FAO proposes new sorghum, cassava, credit projects.
newsitem.headline: FAO proposes new sorghum, cassava, credit projects.

text.p: The U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) on Wednesday outlined proposals for projects to develop the production of sorghum and cassava in Africa and Asia and a special trade credits system for developing nations.
The details were outlined in a paper to the Intergovernmental Group on Grains, a bi-annual meeting attended by more than 50 cereals exporting and importing nations.
It said a $3.2 million four-year sorghum project would be located in Ghana and Nigeria.

"The potential of expanding sorghum production in Africa is considered vast. With the introduction of better agricultural practices and more productive varieties, output could be raised to 25 million tonnes," from 15 million, the paper said.

It proposed a $1.8 million trade credits scheme for Ghana and Zambia designed to boost competitive private trade and introduce public warehousing and inventory credit to give farmers access to trade finance on reasonable terms.
Cassava -- a root, not a grain but brought under the umbrella of the Intergovernmental Group on Grains -- is considered a low-cost commodity that can substitute for expensive cereals imports.
The FAO paper proposed three cassava schemes. One is aimed at boosting the returns of cassava production in south China by increasing technical market information and feasibility studies.

A second project would aim to promote cassava market information and production in Asia and Africa to expand markets and the third is designed to expand cassava utilisation for food, feed and industrial applications in Africa.
Such projects are implemented through the Common Fund for Commodities, an international body which co-finances schemes with local donors, local governments or other international bodies.

"We hope the projects are approved for financing (at the meeting)," Myles Mielke, Secretary of the Interngovernmental Group on Grains, told Reuters before the meeting, which runs until Friday. --Rome newsroom +396 678 2501
